I've had my Panda for a few weeks and it has worked perfectly so far. I keep it in the bathroom where it is easy to hook up the power, water and drain, when finished I disconnect everything and put a folded towel on top which makes a nice extra shelf. I'll continue to go to the laundromat because it would take a long time to process the same amount of clothes you can at the laundry in an hour - pants, shirts, socks, etc. But the Panda is great for small loads. I bought it mostly because I do hot yoga and come home with a bag of soaking wet clothes & towels. They can't wait to be washed, so for a while I've been hand washing in the sink. But with the Panda I can hook up the machine, wash, rinse, spin dry and hang my clothes in about 20 minutes. It's actually kind of fun to use. The spin dryer works very well, it removes so much moisture that I just hang the items in a warm area and they dry in a couple hours. Synthetic fabrics dry very quickly, they are almost dry when they come out. The wash basin and drain pump also work well. The controls are easy to use and allow you to choose how much time to wash, spin or drain. It's also easy to adjust the water temperature, amount of soap and type of rinse from item to item. I add essential oils like tea tree, eucalyptus and cedar to the rinse and spin cycles to sanitize the clothes plus they smell great. Very basic, yet extremely effective machine. The hoses are flimsy but the machine itself seems to be very well built.

This washer/spinner (not dryer) set is kind of remarkable for what it is. The five stars are for overall value, more than anything else.

If you can, your best bet is probably to get a quality, used washer/dryer set delivered. If you're short on space or don't have that option, this is pretty good.

I've done several cycles with mine. Nothing is magical about it, but it just works and seems to put up with some misuse. The spinner is incredibly effective, but the clothes won't be totally dry. You may want a drying rack.

It would've been nice if it came with screw-in hose attachments. I've been using a set of actual washing machine hoses and pointing them into the basin. Pretty much, you control the water temperature by how much hot or cold water you put in. The water level is all you. It just washes and drains. I did keep the lower styrofoam to give it a bit more height (you may want to lift the unit higher for more optimal draining, depending on your configuration) and stability.

I'm not really sure this could be better for the price point. Seems to do a nice job and I haven't killed it yet, so it's doing quite well.

Last tip: You know the spinner is working right when it's not shaking about and it spools up to a very high speed. If not, you may have it overloaded, imbalanced, and/or not have the plastic spacer thing in.

I loved the washer from the start for all the reasons people have listed.
Three months after getting it, the pump broke and I could no longer drain the water. I may have been responsible - while the machine was washing, I kept filling it with water...and forgot all about it. When I remembered, the water had overflowed into the rinse/spinner basin which was now half full. While the washer was still washing, I switched it to drain. I heard it struggle for a second then it started to drain. I turned it off a few minutes later and that was the last time it worked.
I emailed the Amazon seller, First&Best Inc to see if it could be repaired or if there was a pump I could buy. They were incredibly gracious and friendly and accommodating. After troubleshooting the problem with me, they agreed it was the pump, and they immediately send a replacement pump over. It arrived a week later. I replaced it today and it again works like a charm! From now on I will be more gentle with it :-P
But one important thing they didn't explain, which you need to know if you have to replace the pump: You need to disassemble the pump assembly first. The hoses attached to the broken pump can not be removed. They are glued on. Remove the screws from the broken pump - you end up with 2 halves. One half has the hoses attached; the other half has the motor. Take apart the good pump in the same way. Attached the good motor to the hose assembly. Cut the old wires and splice on the new wires

We bought the Panda XPB45 (10 lbs) in Feb 2016. It's now 3 months later and so far so good. It's a good twin-tub washer, compact and rather quiet. Like any twin-tub washer, there's a lot of manual work, like transferring the clothes to the spinner, etc. On the other hand, you can do your laundry exactly the way you want, because you control how long it soaks, washes, how many rinses etc.

Do be aware that the user guide says not to use water hotter than 115F if you use the hose supplied with the machine (120F is the maximum if you fill it with a bucket), so you can't do a 140F standard hot wash in it. The clothes do come clean even with the "hand hot" wash. The user guide also warns against overfilling the wash tub or it can leak on the floor.

The user guide fails to mention one of the most common attributes of twin-tub washers, which is you can do most or all of the rinses in the spinner: you can connect the hose to the spinner side of the machine and open the faucet while it's spinning to do a spray rinse; you can also fill the spin basket with water while it's not running and then spin. While this is not an ideal rinse and you may want to do a final rinse on the washer side once you drain the dirty water and replace it with clean water (and possibly fabric softener), it does make the cycle go faster.

If you want to, you can wash white/light clothing that is not too dirty, spin the clothes while returning the water to the washer side

Washing part is fine. The "drying" part is not good. however long you leave the clothes in the dryer, they will be damp. You'll have to hang all the clothes up and air dry them, so it's pretty much useless.

I recently purchased this compact washer for my cabin in Alaska. I have learned not to overload it and it works very well. I was surprised and very happy with the performance of the spin-dryer. A spin of 3-4 minutes gets clothes sufficiently dry that an hour or two in the breeze or less time hanging on a drying rack behind my wood stove finishes the job. I can put shirts on hangers directly from the spin-dryer and hang in my closet and they are perfectly dry the next day or sooner. If I feel like ironing a shirt or pants they are just damp enough to be ready to iron and dry completely while ironing.

For the summer I have my Panda on my deck near my hot tub and fill itwith a bucket from the tub (thus re-usuing the hot tub water which I then replace - keeping the tub water nice and clean). Since I carry water to this cabin I keep track of usage. A medium load will use about 8 gallons to wash. If you use minimal soap the clothes can be squeezed a bit as you move them to the spin-dryer thus conserving the wash water for a second load (I separate loads washing the cleanest things first when I do this). I then add some water to the spin-dryer while it is spinning at a reported 1400 rpm. My clothes come out nice and fresh.

In winter I will easily move the lightweight Panda inside my cabin where it will fit neatly near my shower, be filled with a hose shower head and drain into the shower base. Like any fairly inexpensive and lightweight product I

Excellent for my small apartment. I just set it up in the bathroom where I can hook the hose up to my sink. However, I used a bucket to draw water from the tube because it would take over an hour to fill just using the plastic hose.

The lint trap needs major improvement; it hardly catches any lint.

To keep the lint from adhering to my clothes and to keep it from catching in the machinery of the draining apparatus of the machine, I use an aquarium fish net to catch free floating lint.
At first, I purchased a small aquarium fish net. It wasn't big enough, so I bought the largest size.

As the load agitates, I hold the aquarium fish net against the side of the tub in the water and catch an amazingly large quantity of lint--cat hair, fabric pile, and fiber--for a 10 lb. load, sometimes up to a cup--I use the "white water" for cleaning the toilet and other household uses. I like conserving resources.

I use a minuscule amount of detergent and ammonia to clean protein, blood, chocolate, coffee stains. If the suds get out of hand even with a small quantity of laundry soap, baking soda helps to 'tame the suds, acts as a softener and freshens the clean clothes.

The I rinse with a cup or two of cleaning vinegar, depending on the size of the load. Vinegar grabs the detergent from the clothes and zaps residue right out of the clothes.

When done, my clothes smell like they been dried outside in the fresh air.

I suspect it's a function of the size of the washing unit versus the agitators. I've taken to putting things like long pants in mesh laundry bags, and I put underwear in some small cotton drawstring bags I happened to have around.

My only real complaint is that I wish the machine had casters on the bottom. It's not that heavy to drag around, but casters would help, and there are places for them. I might add some if I can figure out how.

I bought this item back in May (while still living in a house with a W/D), and used it for the first time earlier today in my new apartment.

I have it set up in my bathroom, on a folded up bath towel to cut down on any vibration and catch any minor leaks. I set up the drainage hose to empty into a 10 gallon bucket, so I could potentially reuse the wash water for a second load.

My first load was 10 T-shirts, with enough water to fill it to the M line (~8 gallons of warm water; filled by hand with a small bucket from the bathtub faucet, plus 1 T laundry detergent). The wash cycle seemed to work fine. Drainage was a bit of a problem, because I discovered that to fully drain the unit, the unit should ideally be a few inches above the end of the drainage hose. Although I could drain about 3/4 of the water into my 10 gallon bucket, the last bit required draining into a shallow bowl (repeatedly dumping and then letting more water drain). This was slightly annoying.

After the wash and drain, when I attempted the rinse cycle, nothing happened. I discovered that I'd blown the circuit breaker on the outlet. Not sure why that happened (it didn't happen for my second load), but after re-setting it I kept a closer eye on it.

The rinse water I drained into the bathtub (still needed the shallow pan to remove the last bit of it). The water still seemed a little grungy, so it made me wonder how clean, or well-rinsed, the clothes really were.

We've washed about a dozen loads in this, so far, and have been very happy with it. We watched a few videos on this machine prior to ordering it, so we knew to expect a little extra work on our part compared to a standard washing machine. The hose fits our kitchen sink without issue, but we also fill the tub with buckets of water. We fill two buckets and set them aside, then hook up the hose to the kitchen faucet and begin filling the tub. While the faucet is filling the tub, we pour in the buckets of water, add detergent and our clothing and wait for the faucet to finish filling the tub to the correct water level. While the clothes are washing/agitating, we fill the buckets again to prepare for the rinse cycle. This saves time on the overall process.
As other reviewers have said, clothes do get twisted. I try to gently untangle them at various stages of the process - usually while the tub is draining/filling. This way clothes don't get too twisted. It hasn't been a big deal for us.
We've been very pleased with our little washer and hope it lasts!
